blocks.text: 1.3 From recovery to growth
At the airport the recovery is complete. Gateway capacity now caps growth in the summer peak, and demand and conversion cap it in the green season.
The limits of recovery logic

The strategy's task is to move the Western Cape from recovery to growth. At the airport the first half is done. International passenger arrivals at Cape Town International reached 1.44m in FY24/25 against 1.16m in FY19/20, and 1.57m in FY25/26 (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p11). On South African Tourism's provincial count the province still stood below 2019 in 2025 (section 1.1).

Recovery logic assumed capacity waiting to be refilled. Arrivals fell to 80,400 in FY20/21 (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p11), and the task was to refill idle seats, rooms and routes. That slack is gone. South Africa's international seat capacity is back at pre-pandemic levels, and Cape Town International shares with Lanseria the highest load factor of the country's five largest airports, 79% across all its seats in 2025 (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "The South African Market").

Cape Town did more than refill its seats. It added 17 mainline international routes between 2015 and 2025, more than any of eight peer airports, and the result is "a 'what next' moment" (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "International Comparisons"; "In Conclusion"). The rebound that a recovery plan is built to capture has already happened.
Seats in summer, demand in winter

Growth is now supply-constrained in the summer peak and demand-constrained in the green season, when airlines withdraw seats. A survey of 34 outbound markets counts 97 million high-value, South Africa-interested travellers, of whom only 1.4 million convert into arrivals (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p41). The conclusion is that "the challenge is not demand generation but improving conversion into actual visits" (p41).

The binding supply is peak capacity at the gateway. The growth model draws current air access as a line at 1.8 million inbound seats, and the base case, in which Wesgro maintains current activity, reaches 1,802,929 arrivals at the 2030 plotted year (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p20). The chart below sets the base case against that line.

blocks.text: The line is the model's assumption, not a measured cap. At the international routes' 76.0% load factor, 1.8 million inbound seats would carry about 1.37 million arrivals, fewer than the 1.57 million ACSA recorded in FY25/26 (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Seasonality"; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p11; computed). The route table counts 3,816,797 international seats for the year to November 2025, more than 1.8 million each way even if that total counts both directions (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Seasonality"). What binds is the runway at peak hours in the summer peak, at about 30 movements an hour (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p101). [Open item: ACSA or OAG to supply peak-hour and seasonal slot headroom at Cape Town International.]

The routes that exist are full. Eleven of the 27 international routes in the load-factor table ran above 80% in the year to November 2025. Together they averaged 76.0% on the printed total, below the airport's 79% across all seats (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Seasonality"). Twenty-nine international routes serve the airport in 2026. Five of the eleven are mature long-haul routes, led by Newark at 88.6%, Atlanta at 84.3% and Frankfurt and London Heathrow at 83.0% ("Seasonality").

Full routes do not add seats of their own accord: "rather than increase capacity carriers will seek to increase revenues via higher selling fares rather than add new services" (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "In Conclusion"). Airlines also pull seats out of winter: June carries 6.4% of the year's international capacity and December 10.8% ("Seasonality").

Behind the routes sits the runway. "The airport, not a shortage of visitors is what now caps Cape Town's tourism growth" (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p101). The single runway caps movements at about 30 an hour until relief arrives in about 2033 (section 1.2).

The secondary gateways do not close the gap in time: "the certain fix is the latest, and the earliest big-capacity option is the least certain" (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p104 to p109). Route rights sit a tier up: air service agreements are a national function (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p58). The Department of Economic Development rates restrictive bilateral agreements a high-impact constraint on airlift (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p24).
Car-only regions and unbookable product

Beyond the Metro the constraint changes shape, not nature: accessibility falls from 4.7 in the Metro to 1.0 in the Central Karoo, and the visitor drives (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p88 to p90, p99).

Much of what the car can reach cannot be booked. Most rural properties have no OTA presence and Route 62 has the lowest online bookability of the six touring routes (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p95, p87). Even CapeNature takes about 70% of its reservations through a call centre rather than its online platform (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p42).
Growth above the norm

Global tourism grows 3% to 5% a year under stable conditions, the band the benchmarking work calls organic growth (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p7). In 2024 the world grew 11% as recovery ran on, and only Chile, at 40.4%, and Singapore, at 21%, grew far faster (UN Tourism, World Tourism Barometer, Jan 2025; Sernatur, Anuario de Turismo 2024, Dec 2025; Singapore Tourism Board, Feb 2025). The longer record is the better test (section 2.1). Santiago's airport grew from about 16 million passengers in 2010 to more than 26 million in 2019, at least 5.5% a year (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p24 to p26; computed).

The Western Cape's two paths straddle the band. The base case implies 3.8% a year from 2025 to 2035 and the accelerated case 5.3%, and the accelerated case reverts to base "without confirmed routes" (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19). Growth counts as structural only above that band, and only when it is "driven by deliberate changes to demand drivers, access conditions or product systems, rather than cyclical recovery or short-term promotion" (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p8).

Cape Town remains "the engine of the system, but growth cannot keep concentrating there" (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p114). The Department of Economic Development already reads the growth framing as overweight on volumes and asks for a value and spend lens in place of arrivals (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p24). Growth now needs new markets, new seasons and new regions, and each of those is a supply problem before it is a marketing problem.
